frozen_original.title: Trump Golf Trips Top 115 Million in Taxpayer Costs on Track for 300 Million by End of Term
frozen_original.synopsis: By August 2026, independent tracker estimates put Trumps second-term golf-related travel and security costs at nearly 115 million dollars, including 80 million for 59 days at Mar-a-Lago and 13.6 million for Bedminster. Trump visited his own properties on 191 of his first 512 days in office, or 37 percent of the time. At his pace the tracker projects 300 million total by end of term, doubling his first-term total.

primary.disposition_rationale: Narrowed the mixed record to the source-supported property-visit frequency. CREW directly reports 191 days out of 512; the unverified $115 million total and $300 million projection are excluded.
primary.title: CREW reported Trump visited profitable properties on 191 of 512 days
primary.description_short: CREW reported that Trump visited resorts and golf courses he profits from on 191 of his first 512 days back in office.
primary.description_medium: CREW's June 16, 2026 tracking reported that Trump visited resorts and golf courses from which he still profits on 191 of his first 512 days back in office, or over one-third of those days. CREW separately counted 259 property visits, including 148 golf-course visits, because multiple properties may be visited on one day. This repair excludes unsupported dollar totals and projections.
primary.description_long: CREW reported on June 16, 2026 that Trump had visited resorts and golf courses he still profits from on 191 of his first 512 days after returning to office, or over one-third of those days. CREW separately counted 259 property visits, including 148 golf-course visits, because Trump can visit more than one property in a day. This repair uses the reported day count and preserves the distinction between days with a visit and individual property visits. CREW says trips produce taxpayer spending at businesses he owns and profits from, but the reviewed source does not supply an auditable second-term total for the travel and security claims in the frozen entry. The $115 million figure, the $300 million end-of-term projection, the $80 million Mar-a-Lago breakdown, and the Bedminster amount therefore remain outside the repaired copy. No amount or forecast is treated as established. This entry records the reported frequency and the connection to properties from which Trump profits, while leaving public cost unquantified.
primary.date_precision: Reported through June 16, 2026; date range reflects CREW's 512-day period beginning after the January 2025 return to office.
primary.subcategory: Presidential travel to privately profitable properties
organization_tags: Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington

frozen_original.title: Trump Proposes Using Military Courts to Try Civilian Immigration Cases
frozen_original.synopsis: The Trump administration floated a proposal in February 2025 to use military tribunals to adjudicate civilian immigration cases, bypassing the federal immigration court system, which had a massive backlog. The proposal was immediately flagged as unconstitutional, as military courts have no jurisdiction over civilian matters under the Uniform Code of Military Justice. Constitutional scholars warned that subjecting civilians to military justice is a defining characteristic of authoritarian and martial law regimes. The proposal was never formally implemented but signaled the administration's willingness to consider military law as a solution to civilian legal obstacles.

The packet gives no originating memo, named official, quoted announcement, court filing, or source URL establishing that this proposal was made. It therefore cannot support a factual account of who proposed the idea, what legal mechanism was contemplated, who would be covered, or whether any agency acted on it. The proposal must not be described as an enacted policy, tribunal proceeding, or settled administration decision. A February 2025 report found during research discussed an outside contractor’s mass-deportation plan and proposals for mass immigration hearings, not military tribunals; it is a different proposal and does not substantiate this entry. Day-level timing, authorship, scope, legal analysis, and any subsequent action are unknown. frozen_original.title: Trump Issues Broad Self-Pardon Covering All Crimes During His First Term
frozen_original.synopsis: On January 20, 2025 — his first day back in office — Donald Trump issued a presidential self-pardon purporting to cover any and all federal crimes he may have committed from January 20, 2017 through January 20, 2021, the duration of his first term. The self-pardon was an unprecedented exercise of presidential clemency power with no historical precedent in American history; no prior president had ever pardoned themselves, and constitutional scholars had long debated whether the Constitution's pardon clause permitted self-pardons at all. Trump accompanied the self-pardon with pardons for all January 6 Capitol rioters. Legal scholars were divided on the self-pardon's constitutional validity, with many arguing it would fail judicial review. Nevertheless, the act of pardoning oneself represented a brazen assertion that the president placed himself above criminal accountability — a claim incompatible with the foundational principle that no person is above the law.

It also asserts that he pardoned January 6 defendants on the same day and describes the self-pardon as constitutionally disputed. The supplied blocker directly contradicts the central event: it says prior research found no public record of a Trump self-pardon and that Department of Justice clemency records listed pardons for January 6 defendants but no pardon of Trump himself. Those prior notes include no source URL, record excerpt, or instrument available for this repair, so they are not treated as independently checked proof of absence. The separate January 6 clemency assertion does not establish that the president pardoned himself and should not bridge that gap. This draft retains the self-pardon only as the supplied record’s unverified allegation. It does not claim that a self-pardon occurred, that it covered all first-term crimes, or that a court assessed its validity. The exact date, document, legal scope, and any corroborating record remain unknown. Do not publish unless a matching clemency instrument or reliable contemporaneous evidence is produced.

frozen_original.title: Trump's Emoluments Clause Violations
frozen_original.synopsis: Trump's crypto, airplane, and other grifts may violate the emoluments clause, which prohibits government officials from accepting gifts or benefits from foreign governments. This has raised concerns about the potential for self-enrichment and abuse of power. The Trump administration's actions have been criticized for being corrupt and unethical. The emoluments clause is seen as a key check on the president's power and a safeguard against corruption.
